# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive Summary

Public sources describe Conti as a large, professionally organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation rather than a loose collection of independent criminals. The available record portrays a group that developed and maintained ransomware, recruited technical personnel, used affiliates or other third parties for intrusions, and monetized attacks through data theft, encryption, ransom negotiation, and threatened publication of stolen information. The Center for Internet Security (CIS) characterizes the RaaS model as one in which developers lease malware to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The February–March 2022 ContiLeaks disclosures exposed internal communications, organizational practices, technical-development discussions, alleged financial information, and operational-security failures. Rapid7 reported that the initial disclosure included approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs distributed across 393 JSON files, although some material was encrypted and therefore not fully reviewable. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2) CIS’s account of the leaks describes distinct internal functions—including coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, and penetration testers or hackers—and reports that an insider estimated the organization employed more than 60 people in July 2021. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The public attribution record has two separate components. First, the U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice program publicly assesses that the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are linked to Conti and Wizard Spider. It offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government who participate in qualifying malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1) Second, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. The supplied DOJ record does not, however, state that any of these defendants used one of the five Rewards for Justice aliases. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

The strongest conclusion supported by the sources is therefore that Conti was publicly documented as a commercialized, technically staffed RaaS ecosystem, while attribution to specific individuals remains divided between a reward notice naming online aliases and a DOJ case page naming charged defendants. The supplied evidence does not establish a one-to-one identity match between those aliases and defendants.

## Source Assessment and Scope

The sources differ in institutional role and evidentiary character:

| Source | Institutional character | Main contribution | Evidentiary limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rewards for Justice | U.S. government reward and attribution notice | Names five aliases, associates them with Conti/Wizard Spider, and describes the U.S. government’s assessment of the threat | Uses terms such as “believed to be linked”; does not identify the aliases’ legal names in the supplied text |
| Rapid7 | Cybersecurity company threat-research analysis | Describes the ContiLeaks archive, internal chats, technical practices, and operational response | Reports some leaked material as incomplete or unverified; expressly says it did not access exposed remote systems |
| CIS/MS-ISAC perspective | Nonprofit cybersecurity organization and information-sharing network | Explains RaaS commercialization and summarizes organizational findings from the leaks | Relies partly on open-source reporting and interviews rather than a judicial finding |
| DOJ, Middle District of Tennessee | U.S. federal law-enforcement case record | Names defendants, case numbers, charges, plea information, and victim-notification details | Charges are allegations unless and until proven; the page does not provide a complete evidentiary narrative or alias mapping |

This report treats government assessments as assessments, leaked-chat interpretations as reporting, and criminal charges as allegations unless the supplied record expressly reports a plea or conviction. The DOJ page states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

## How Public Sources Describe Conti’s RaaS Model

### Commercial organization and division of labor

CIS describes ransomware commercialization as a shift toward organizational structures resembling legitimate businesses. These structures may include recruiting or human-resources functions, finance and accounting, and personnel who negotiate ransom payments. In the RaaS model, developers provide or lease malware to affiliates, affiliates conduct victim intrusions, and the parties share revenue. CIS identifies a commonly reported split as approximately 70 percent to affiliates and 30 percent to developers, while presenting that split as a general model rather than a finding necessarily applicable to every Conti transaction. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The significance of this model is operational scalability. Initial-access brokers can sell already established access to victim environments, reducing the time that affiliates must spend penetrating networks. Affiliates can then focus on deploying ransomware and pursuing payment, while the core organization can concentrate on developing, testing, and improving the malware. CIS’s MS-ISAC interview explains that this separation can increase the number of potential victims and allow the core operators to offload some operational risk. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The supplied Rewards for Justice page describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group that targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. This is a U.S. government characterization; the page does not provide a detailed legal or intelligence basis for the “government-linked” description. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

### Double extortion and victim pressure

The public descriptions consistently identify a double-extortion model. According to Rewards for Justice, Conti operators typically stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations. The ransom process directed victims to contact the actors through an online portal; if payment was not made, the stolen data could be sold or published on a site controlled by Conti actors. The same page reports that ransom demands varied substantially, with some reaching as high as $25 million. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

CIS likewise describes Conti as a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion. The DOJ record describes Conti ransomware as malicious software that affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and elsewhere. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

Rewards for Justice reports a broader figure: more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure, and more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, including more than 290 in the United States. These figures concern operations and organizations, whereas the DOJ’s “more than 900” figure concerns affected entities. Because the sources use different measures, the numbers should not be treated as directly interchangeable. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

### Malware and associated tools

Rewards for Justice associates Conti with Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. The page labels Conti and Wizard Spider as associated cyberthreat organizations and lists those applications as associated malicious cyber applications. The supplied text does not explain the precise relationship between Conti and each listed application; therefore, the listing supports association, not necessarily authorship or exclusive control. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

Rapid7 reports that Conti’s internal discussions addressed ransomware features, encryption of very large files, endpoint-detection testing, command-and-control infrastructure, malicious documents, and methods for delivering ransomware without detection by dynamic analysis. Rapid7 also reports that the group used phishing as one initial-access method. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

## What the Leaks Exposed

### The ContiLeaks disclosure

Rapid7 reports that, on February 27, 2022, the account known as @ContiLeaks released a large collection of internal Conti chat logs after Conti publicly expressed support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 states that some Conti members supported Ukraine, creating internal conflict, and that Conti later revised its public message. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

The initial archive reportedly contained 393 JSON files and approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs. The material included internal communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of exploits and design processes. Rapid7 cautioned that some messages were encrypted, making the available information incomplete. It also reported that later disclosures included usernames, passwords, alleged access details for command-and-control and storage servers, and a file purported to be Conti source code. Rapid7 explicitly stated that it did not access the remote systems and recommended against using the disclosed credentials. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

### Internal departments and personnel

The leaks depicted Conti as a structured organization with specialized roles. CIS, summarizing research on the disclosures, identifies “Coders” who wrote malicious code and integrated technologies; “Testers” who evaluated ransomware against security products; “Administrators”; “Reverse Engineers”; and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted outside the organization. CIS also reports that departments had their own budgets and could borrow funds from one another. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

CIS reports an insider estimate of more than 60 employees in July 2021, primarily coders and testers. It also states that staffing levels changed, including dismissals after internal security breaches. This supports the conclusion that Conti possessed persistent organizational roles and management practices, but the exact headcount should be treated as an insider estimate rather than a verified personnel census. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

### Product development and spending

The leaks showed efforts to improve the ransomware product and its ability to evade security controls. CIS reports that Conti allocated $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license, budgeted several thousand dollars monthly for security and antivirus software used by testers, and redirected reverse engineers in July 2021 toward Windows 11. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

Rapid7 similarly describes Conti as operating like a software company, with technical discussions about feature development, encryption performance, endpoint-detection products, and deployment logistics. Rapid7 also reports that internal chats included salary negotiations, technical coding exercises, product-status discussions, and out-of-office messages. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

Rapid7 reports that the leaked chats identified a primary Bitcoin address allegedly containing more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. This is a reported interpretation of leaked financial information, not a judicially established balance in the supplied evidence. Rapid7 also reports a conversation suggesting possible FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in information relating to Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. Because the material is incomplete and the supplied source characterizes the implication rather than presenting an adjudicated finding, those points should remain allegations or assessments. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

## Law-Enforcement Attribution and Defendant Record

### Rewards for Justice aliases

Rewards for Justice names five online aliases: “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis.” It states that malicious cyber actors known by these aliases are believed to be linked to Conti. The page also associates Conti with Wizard Spider and lists Russia as an associated location. The wording “believed to be linked” signals a government attribution assessment rather than a criminal adjudication identifying each alias’s legal identity. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

The reward is up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The supplied page does not say that every person using one of the five aliases has been legally established to satisfy every element of that description. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

### DOJ defendants and case status

The DOJ page identifies two cases. Case No. 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The page states that, on September 7, 2023, these defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

Case No. 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. The DOJ page states that he was charged in connection with a conspiracy to deploy Conti, which infected computers and networks and encrypted data. It further reports that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement, and was scheduled for sentencing on September 10, 2026. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

The supplied DOJ record does not identify any of the five Rewards for Justice aliases as belonging to Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko. Nor does it state that the defendants are the same persons described in the Rewards for Justice notice. Accordingly, a responsible attribution report must keep the alias-based and defendant-based records distinct.

## Contradictions, Gaps, and Uncertainty

The sources present different victim and operation counts: Rewards for Justice reports more than 1,000 operations and more than 400 affected organizations, while DOJ reports more than 900 affected victims. These figures may reflect different definitions, reporting periods, or counting methods. The record does not provide enough information to reconcile them definitively. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

There is also a temporal distinction between Rapid7’s March 2022 assessment that Conti remained active and significant after the leak and CIS’s later account that the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units in 2022. These statements are not necessarily contradictory: one concerns activity immediately after the leak, while the other concerns later dismantling and fragmentation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2; [Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The principal unresolved gap is identity resolution. The available sources link five aliases to Conti but do not connect them to the DOJ defendants. The DOJ page names defendants and charges but does not provide their online aliases. Any assertion that an alias belongs to a named defendant would exceed the supplied evidence.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a concrete assessment: Conti was publicly described as a mature RaaS enterprise whose criminal capacity depended on specialization, affiliate-based operations, technical development, testing, professionalized administration, and double-extortion monetization. The ContiLeaks disclosures materially strengthened that assessment by exposing internal hiring, budgeting, technical-development, and security-testing practices. They also revealed the risks created by centralized communications and poor operational security.

The attribution record is credible but layered rather than complete. Rewards for Justice provides a U.S. government assessment linking “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” to Conti/Wizard Spider and offers a reward for information concerning qualifying malicious cyber activity. DOJ records separately document Conti-related criminal cases against five named defendants, including charges against four defendants and a reported guilty plea by Lytvynenko. The available sources do not establish that the aliases and defendants are identical. That distinction is essential: public attribution to an online alias, a government threat assessment, a criminal charge, and a guilty plea are different evidentiary categories.

## References

Center for Internet Security. (2022). *The Conti leaks: A case of cybercrime’s commercialization*. CIS. [https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)

Rapid7. (2022, March 1). *Conti ransomware group internal chats leaked over Russia-Ukraine conflict*. Rapid7 Blog. [https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)

U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee. (2026). *Conti ransomware*. [https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)
